Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 26, verses 1–9:

Meccan, except His words ﴿And the poets—the deviators follow them﴾ to the end of the surah, which is Medinan. It contains five thousand five hundred and forty-two letters, one thousand two hundred and ninety-seven words, and two hundred and twenty-seven verses.

Abu al-Husayn al-Khabbazi informed us, saying: Abu al-Shaykh al-Isfahani narrated to us, saying: Abu al-'Abbas al-Tahrani narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Ya'la ibn Mansur narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Abi Uways narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, from Abu Bakr, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned from the first Remembrance (al-dhikr al-awwal). I was given Ta-Ha and the Ta-Sin surahs from the tablets of Musa (peace be upon him). I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the closings of the surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned from beneath the Throne. And I was given the Mufassal as a bonus (nafilah)." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 13/87.]

Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Mawardi al-Farisi informed me, saying: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Mansur al-Khayzurani narrated to us in Baghdad, saying: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Habib narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub ibn Yusuf narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Kharijah informed us, from 'Abd Allah, from Isma'il ibn Abi Rafi', from al-Raqashi and from al-Hasan, from Anas, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah gave me the seven (long surahs) in place of the Torah, and He gave me the Ta-Sin surahs in place of the Psalms. He favoured me with the Hawamim and the Mufassal, which no prophet before me has recited." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 13/87, with the addition: "And He gave me al-Mubin in place of the Gospel."]

Kamil ibn Ahmad al-Nahwi and Sa'id ibn Muhammad al-Muqri informed us, the two of them saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Shurutti informed us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Sharik al-Kufi narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Yarbu'i narrated to us, saying: Salam ibn Sulaym narrated to us, saying: Harun ibn Kathir narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, Abu Umamah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Whoever recites the surah of al-Shu'ara' will have ten good deeds for each person who believed in Nuh and denied him, and Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih and Ibrahim, and for each person who denied 'Isa and believed in Muhammad (ﷺ)." [93] [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 5/239.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Sin-Mim.﴾ The reciters differed regarding it and its two companions (in the other surahs). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and 'Asim in some transmissions read the ta with kasrah, using imalah (vowel inclination). The people of Medina read it between the kasrah and the fathah, and this was the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. Others read it with fathah, using tafkhim (emphatic articulation). Abu Ja'far and Hamzah made the nun in the sin audible here and in Surat al-Qasas, for clarity and firmness, while the others concealed it because the sin is adjacent to letters of the mouth. As for its interpretation: al-Walibi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ta-Sin-Mim" is an oath, and it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted. 'Ikrimah narrated from him: The scholars were unable to know its tafsir. Mujahid said: It is the name of the surah. Qatadah and Abu Rawq said: It is one of the names of the Qur'an, by which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, swore. Al-Qurazi said: Allah swore by His length, His elevation and His dominion.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hanash narrated to us [in the second copy: Habash al-Muqri], saying: Ahmad ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Yahya al-Darimi narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Abdah al-Misisi narrated to me, saying: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Firyabi narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Bishr al-Raqqi narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Umar Hafs ibn Maysarah narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil, from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: When this verse "Ta-Sin-Mim" was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The ta is Tur Sina', the sin is Alexandria, and the mim is Makkah." [Zad al-Masir: 6/30.] [94]

Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: The ta is Tuba, the sin is Sidrat al-Muntaha, and the mim is Muhammad the Chosen (ﷺ).

﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ That is: these are the verses of the Book that makes things clear. ﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself with grief (la'allaka bakhi'un nafsaka) that they do not believe.﴾ That is, perhaps you will destroy yourself. This was when the people of Makkah denied him, and it grieved him, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse. Its parallel is in al-Kahf.

﴿If We wish, We could send down upon them a sign from the sky, so that their necks would remain bowed (fazallat a'naquhum laha khadi'in)﴾, humbled. He said: If Allah, the Exalted, willed, He would send down upon them a sign by which they would be humbled, so that none of them would turn his neck toward disobedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Ibn Jurayj said: If He willed, He would show them a matter of His command, and none of them would act in disobedience.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hibban narrated to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn 'Isa [in the second copy: Ibrahim ibn Ishaq] narrated to us, saying: 'Ali ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Abu Hamzah al-Thumali narrated to me concerning this verse, saying: "It has reached us, and Allah knows best, that it is a voice heard from the sky on the middle of the month of Ramadan, at which the young women come out of their houses."

And with this chain, from Abu Hamzah, who said: al-Kalbi narrated to me, from Abu Salih, the mawla of Umm Hani, that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas told him: This verse was revealed about us and about the Banu Umayyah. He said: "There will come for us a dominion over them, and their necks will be humbled before us after hardship, and debasement after might."

As for His words ﴿khadi'in﴾, in the masculine plural, and not "khadi'ah", the feminine, though the attribute refers to ﴿a'naq﴾ (necks), there are sound interpretations: First: the meaning is "the owners of the necks were humbled by it (fazalla ashab al-a'naq laha khadi'in)." The word "owners" is omitted and "necks" stands in its place, because when necks are humbled, their possessors are humbled. The verb is first attributed to the necks, then "humbled" is attributed to men, like the words of the poet:

"Upon a clenched hand whose back was bent, so that the man is neither ashamed nor eating."

Here the verb relating to "the back" is feminine, because the palm includes the back and is sufficient for it, just as you are content to say "I submitted to the command" by saying "my neck submitted to you." The Arabs say: "Every one who has an eye looks at you (kull dhi 'ayn nazir ilayk)" and "nazirah ilayk" (feminine), because your saying "my eye looked at you" and "I looked at you" have one meaning. This is common in Arabic speech: the predicate is left aside from the first noun and directed to the second, which takes the predicate, like the words of the rajaz poet:

"The lengths of the nights hastened my wearing away; they wore out my length and my breadth."

He reports about "the nights" and omits "length" (tul). Jarir said:

"I see the passing of years has taken from me, as the crescent loses its light from the moon."

Al-Farazdaq said:

"We see their spears carried by them when the iron rusts upon the warriors."

He did not make the predicate apply to the spears, but returned it to "them," the pronoun of the people. This is permissible because if "length" and "spears" were dropped from the sentence, the meaning would not be corrupted by their omission. Likewise, the verb is returned to the pronoun in His words ﴿a'naquhum﴾, because if "the necks" were dropped, the sentence would not be corrupted, and what remains would convey the meaning, so it would be "fazallu khadi'ina laha." Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd relied on this view.

Others said: The attribute was mentioned because of its proximity to the masculine word ﴿hum﴾, following the Arab custom of masculinizing a feminine noun when it is attached to a masculine one, and feminizing a masculine noun when it is attached to a feminine one. Like the words of al-A'sha:

"And you choke on the word you have spread, as the spear's tip chokes on blood."

And al-'Ajjaj said:

"When he saw the back of the sky had moved away."

It was also said: Since humbling is what is familiar among the sons of Adam, He presented the necks in the manner of the sons of Adam, like His words ﴿And the sun and the moon—I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 4], and His words, Exalted is He, ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 18]. And from this is the words of the poet:

"I sipped it while the rooster called to its morning, when the stars of the Bier had drawn near and then turned away."

It was also said: He said ﴿khadi'in﴾ [in the second copy an addition: "for the sake of the ends of verses, so that they would be of one pattern; and it was said: He meant: fazallu khadi'in"], so He expressed the whole bodies by the necks, and the Arabs express a part of a thing by the whole of it, as in His words ﴿because of what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Surah al-Hajj: 10], and His words ﴿We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [Surah al-Isra': 13], and similar.

Mujahid said: By "the necks" here he meant the leaders and the great ones. It was also said: By "the necks" he meant the groups and the companies of people. It is said: "The people came 'unuqan," meaning in groups and bands, like the words of the poet:

"Indeed, Iraq and its people are a 'unuq (group) turned toward you, so hayt hayta!"

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: fazallat a'naquhum laha khadi'ah.

﴿And there does not come to them any reminder (dhikr)﴾, that is, any admonition or exhortation ﴿from the Most Gracious, newly revealed (muhdath)﴾ in the revelation and the sending down, ﴿but they turn away from it﴾, ﴿so they have denied, and the news (anba') will come to them﴾, that is, reports, consequences and recompense, ﴿of that which they used to mock.﴾ This is a warning to them. ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many of every noble (karim) kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ That is, every color and kind of plant that people and livestock eat. Karim means good, honoured by people. It is said: "a noble palm tree" when its fruit is good, and "a noble she-camel" when her milk is abundant.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Bakhtawayh narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Thawr and Ibrahim ibn Abi Yusuf [in the second copy: Ibn Abi Sufyan] narrated to us, the two of them saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Ghazali narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from a man, from al-Sha'bi, concerning His words ﴿We caused to grow therein from every noble kind﴾, who said: "The people are from the growth of the earth. Whoever enters Paradise is noble, and whoever enters the Fire is base."

﴿Indeed, in that which I have mentioned there is surely a sign (ayah)﴾, that is, a proof of My existence, My oneness, and the perfection of My power and wisdom. ﴿But most of them are not believers﴾, because of what preceded in My knowledge about them. Sibawayh said: here "kana" is a redundant particle (silah); its meaning is: "and most of them are not believers." ﴿And indeed your Lord—He is surely the Almighty (al-'Aziz), who takes revenge on His enemies, the Most Merciful (al-Rahim), who is full of mercy toward His allies.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Sin-Mim.﴾ The reciters differed regarding it and its two companions (in the other surahs). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and 'Asim in some transmissions read the ta with kasrah, using imalah (vowel inclination). The people of Medina read it between the kasrah and the fathah, and this was the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. Others read it with fathah, using tafkhim (emphatic articulation). Abu Ja'far and Hamzah made the nun in the sin audible here and in Surat al-Qasas, for clarity and firmness, while the others concealed it because the sin is adjacent to letters of the mouth. As for its interpretation: al-Walibi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ta-Sin-Mim" is an oath, and it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted. 'Ikrimah narrated from him: The scholars were unable to know its tafsir. Mujahid said: It is the name of the surah. Qatadah and Abu Rawq said: It is one of the names of the Qur'an, by which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, swore. Al-Qurazi said: Allah swore by His length, His elevation and His dominion.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hanash narrated to us [in the second copy: Habash al-Muqri], saying: Ahmad ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Yahya al-Darimi narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Abdah al-Misisi narrated to me, saying: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Firyabi narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Bishr al-Raqqi narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Umar Hafs ibn Maysarah narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil, from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: When this verse "Ta-Sin-Mim" was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The ta is Tur Sina', the sin is Alexandria, and the mim is Makkah." [Zad al-Masir: 6/30.] [94]

Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: The ta is Tuba, the sin is Sidrat al-Muntaha, and the mim is Muhammad the Chosen (ﷺ).

﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ That is: these are the verses of the Book that makes things clear. ﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself with grief (la'allaka bakhi'un nafsaka) that they do not believe.﴾ That is, perhaps you will destroy yourself. This was when the people of Makkah denied him, and it grieved him, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse. Its parallel is in al-Kahf.

﴿If We wish, We could send down upon them a sign from the sky, so that their necks would remain bowed (fazallat a'naquhum laha khadi'in)﴾, humbled. He said: If Allah, the Exalted, willed, He would send down upon them a sign by which they would be humbled, so that none of them would turn his neck toward disobedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Ibn Jurayj said: If He willed, He would show them a matter of His command, and none of them would act in disobedience.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hibban narrated to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn 'Isa [in the second copy: Ibrahim ibn Ishaq] narrated to us, saying: 'Ali ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Abu Hamzah al-Thumali narrated to me concerning this verse, saying: "It has reached us, and Allah knows best, that it is a voice heard from the sky on the middle of the month of Ramadan, at which the young women come out of their houses."

And with this chain, from Abu Hamzah, who said: al-Kalbi narrated to me, from Abu Salih, the mawla of Umm Hani, that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas told him: This verse was revealed about us and about the Banu Umayyah. He said: "There will come for us a dominion over them, and their necks will be humbled before us after hardship, and debasement after might."

As for His words ﴿khadi'in﴾, in the masculine plural, and not "khadi'ah", the feminine, though the attribute refers to ﴿a'naq﴾ (necks), there are sound interpretations: First: the meaning is "the owners of the necks were humbled by it (fazalla ashab al-a'naq laha khadi'in)." The word "owners" is omitted and "necks" stands in its place, because when necks are humbled, their possessors are humbled. The verb is first attributed to the necks, then "humbled" is attributed to men, like the words of the poet:

"Upon a clenched hand whose back was bent, so that the man is neither ashamed nor eating."

Here the verb relating to "the back" is feminine, because the palm includes the back and is sufficient for it, just as you are content to say "I submitted to the command" by saying "my neck submitted to you." The Arabs say: "Every one who has an eye looks at you (kull dhi 'ayn nazir ilayk)" and "nazirah ilayk" (feminine), because your saying "my eye looked at you" and "I looked at you" have one meaning. This is common in Arabic speech: the predicate is left aside from the first noun and directed to the second, which takes the predicate, like the words of the rajaz poet:

"The lengths of the nights hastened my wearing away; they wore out my length and my breadth."

He reports about "the nights" and omits "length" (tul). Jarir said:

"I see the passing of years has taken from me, as the crescent loses its light from the moon."

Al-Farazdaq said:

"We see their spears carried by them when the iron rusts upon the warriors."

He did not make the predicate apply to the spears, but returned it to "them," the pronoun of the people. This is permissible because if "length" and "spears" were dropped from the sentence, the meaning would not be corrupted by their omission. Likewise, the verb is returned to the pronoun in His words ﴿a'naquhum﴾, because if "the necks" were dropped, the sentence would not be corrupted, and what remains would convey the meaning, so it would be "fazallu khadi'ina laha." Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd relied on this view.

Others said: The attribute was mentioned because of its proximity to the masculine word ﴿hum﴾, following the Arab custom of masculinizing a feminine noun when it is attached to a masculine one, and feminizing a masculine noun when it is attached to a feminine one. Like the words of al-A'sha:

"And you choke on the word you have spread, as the spear's tip chokes on blood."

And al-'Ajjaj said:

"When he saw the back of the sky had moved away."

It was also said: Since humbling is what is familiar among the sons of Adam, He presented the necks in the manner of the sons of Adam, like His words ﴿And the sun and the moon—I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 4], and His words, Exalted is He, ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 18]. And from this is the words of the poet:

"I sipped it while the rooster called to its morning, when the stars of the Bier had drawn near and then turned away."

It was also said: He said ﴿khadi'in﴾ [in the second copy an addition: "for the sake of the ends of verses, so that they would be of one pattern; and it was said: He meant: fazallu khadi'in"], so He expressed the whole bodies by the necks, and the Arabs express a part of a thing by the whole of it, as in His words ﴿because of what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Surah al-Hajj: 10], and His words ﴿We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [Surah al-Isra': 13], and similar.

Mujahid said: By "the necks" here he meant the leaders and the great ones. It was also said: By "the necks" he meant the groups and the companies of people. It is said: "The people came 'unuqan," meaning in groups and bands, like the words of the poet:

"Indeed, Iraq and its people are a 'unuq (group) turned toward you, so hayt hayta!"

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: fazallat a'naquhum laha khadi'ah.

﴿And there does not come to them any reminder (dhikr)﴾, that is, any admonition or exhortation ﴿from the Most Gracious, newly revealed (muhdath)﴾ in the revelation and the sending down, ﴿but they turn away from it﴾, ﴿so they have denied, and the news (anba') will come to them﴾, that is, reports, consequences and recompense, ﴿of that which they used to mock.﴾ This is a warning to them. ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many of every noble (karim) kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ That is, every color and kind of plant that people and livestock eat. Karim means good, honoured by people. It is said: "a noble palm tree" when its fruit is good, and "a noble she-camel" when her milk is abundant.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Bakhtawayh narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Thawr and Ibrahim ibn Abi Yusuf [in the second copy: Ibn Abi Sufyan] narrated to us, the two of them saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Ghazali narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from a man, from al-Sha'bi, concerning His words ﴿We caused to grow therein from every noble kind﴾, who said: "The people are from the growth of the earth. Whoever enters Paradise is noble, and whoever enters the Fire is base."

﴿Indeed, in that which I have mentioned there is surely a sign (ayah)﴾, that is, a proof of My existence, My oneness, and the perfection of My power and wisdom. ﴿But most of them are not believers﴾, because of what preceded in My knowledge about them. Sibawayh said: here "kana" is a redundant particle (silah); its meaning is: "and most of them are not believers." ﴿And indeed your Lord—He is surely the Almighty (al-'Aziz), who takes revenge on His enemies, the Most Merciful (al-Rahim), who is full of mercy toward His allies.﴾

"Upon a clenched hand whose back was bent, so that the man is neither ashamed nor eating."

This is permissible because if "length" and "spears" were dropped from the sentence, the meaning would not be corrupted by their omission. Likewise, the verb is returned to the pronoun in His words ﴿a'naquhum﴾, because if "the necks" were dropped, the sentence would not be corrupted, and what remains would convey the meaning, so it would be "fazallu khadi'ina laha." Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd relied on this view.

Others said: The attribute was mentioned because of its proximity to the masculine word ﴿hum﴾, following the Arab custom of masculinizing a feminine noun when it is attached to a masculine one, and feminizing a masculine noun when it is attached to a feminine one. Like the words of al-A'sha:

"And you choke on the word you have spread, as the spear's tip chokes on blood."

And al-'Ajjaj said:

"When he saw the back of the sky had moved away."

It was also said: Since humbling is what is familiar among the sons of Adam, He presented the necks in the manner of the sons of Adam, like His words ﴿And the sun and the moon—I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 4], and His words, Exalted is He, ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 18]. And from this is the words of the poet:

"I sipped it while the rooster called to its morning, when the stars of the Bier had drawn near and then turned away."

It was also said: He said ﴿khadi'in﴾ [in the second copy an addition: "for the sake of the ends of verses, so that they would be of one pattern; and it was said: He meant: fazallu khadi'in"], so He expressed the whole bodies by the necks, and the Arabs express a part of a thing by the whole of it, as in His words ﴿because of what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Surah al-Hajj: 10], and His words ﴿We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [Surah al-Isra': 13], and similar.

Mujahid said: By "the necks" here he meant the leaders and the great ones. It was also said: By "the necks" he meant the groups and the companies of people. It is said: "The people came 'unuqan," meaning in groups and bands, like the words of the poet:

"Indeed, Iraq and its people are a 'unuq (group) turned toward you, so hayt hayta!"

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: fazallat a'naquhum laha khadi'ah.

﴿And there does not come to them any reminder (dhikr)﴾, that is, any admonition or exhortation ﴿from the Most Gracious, newly revealed (muhdath)﴾ in the revelation and the sending down, ﴿but they turn away from it﴾, ﴿so they have denied, and the news (anba') will come to them﴾, that is, reports, consequences and recompense, ﴿of that which they used to mock.﴾ This is a warning to them. ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many of every noble (karim) kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ That is, every color and kind of plant that people and livestock eat. Karim means good, honoured by people. It is said: "a noble palm tree" when its fruit is good, and "a noble she-camel" when her milk is abundant.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Bakhtawayh narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Thawr and Ibrahim ibn Abi Yusuf [in the second copy: Ibn Abi Sufyan] narrated to us, the two of them saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Ghazali narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from a man, from al-Sha'bi, concerning His words ﴿We caused to grow therein from every noble kind﴾, who said: "The people are from the growth of the earth. Whoever enters Paradise is noble, and whoever enters the Fire is base."

﴿Indeed, in that which I have mentioned there is surely a sign (ayah)﴾, that is, a proof of My existence, My oneness, and the perfection of My power and wisdom. ﴿But most of them are not believers﴾, because of what preceded in My knowledge about them. Sibawayh said: here "kana" is a redundant particle (silah); its meaning is: "and most of them are not believers." ﴿And indeed your Lord—He is surely the Almighty (al-'Aziz), who takes revenge on His enemies, the Most Merciful (al-Rahim), who is full of mercy toward His allies.﴾

And [remember, O Muhammad,] when your Lord called out to Moses when he saw the tree and the fire, saying: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾, those who wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience, and the Children of Israel, whom they enslaved and subjected to a harsh torment.

﴿The people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear God?﴾ Ubayd ibn Umayr read it with the letter *tā'* (تتقون, "will you not fear God?"), meaning: say to them both, "Will you not fear God?"

He said: ﴿My Lord, I fear that they will deny me﴾, and ﴿my breast will be constricted﴾ by their denial of me, ﴿and my tongue will not be loosed﴾ for speech and conveying the message, because of the knot that is in it. The common reading has the two verbs (*yakdhibūn*, *yaḍīqu*) and (*yanṭaliqu*) with *ḍamma* on the *qāf*s, as a continuation of *akhāfu*. Ya'qub read them in the accusative, on the meaning of "that they will deny me, and that my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed." ﴿So send [word] to Aaron﴾ to support me and back me in conveying the message. This is like your saying: "When a calamity befalls me, I send to you," meaning: so that you may help me. ﴿And they have a charge against me﴾, meaning the killing he committed among them. His name was Mathun, and he was Pharaoh's baker. It is also said that the meaning is "with me," i.e., "they have a charge with me." ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ because of it.

God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿No!﴾, meaning: they will not kill you. ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs; indeed We are with you, listening﴾, hearing what they say and what is said to you. He intended by this to strengthen their hearts and to inform them that He would help and protect them. ﴿Go to Pharaoh and say: "Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾

He did not say "messenger" (*rasūlan*, singular) because he meant the verbal noun, i.e., "a message." Its figurative sense is: "one who has a message from the Lord of the worlds," as in the verse of Kuthayyir:

"The slanderers have lied; I did not disclose a secret to them, nor did I send them as a messenger."

i.e., with a message. Al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Except whoever conveys from us to Khafaf, a messenger, the house of your family its destination."

meaning "a message," therefore it is said "its destination." This was said by al-Farra'.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the word *rasūl* may be used for the singular, the dual and the plural. The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent, these two are my messenger and my agent, these are my messenger and my agent." From this is God's saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾. It is also said that the meaning is: each of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.

[Pharaoh is told:] ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., to Palestine, and do not enslave them. Pharaoh had enslaved them for four hundred years, and at that time they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. Moses set out for Egypt, and Aaron was there, and he informed him of this. So they both went together to Pharaoh, but they were not admitted to see him for a year. Then the doorkeeper entered and said to Pharaoh: "There is a man here who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him." So they both entered upon him and delivered to him the message of God, glory be to Him, and Pharaoh recognised Moses, for he had been raised in his house. So he said to him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life﴾, and they were thirty years, ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾, meaning the killing of the Copt.

Ibn 'Abdus informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm related to us, saying: al-Farra' related to us, saying: Musa al-Ansari related to me, from al-Sari ibn Isma'il, from al-Sha'bi, that he read ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾ with a *kasra* on the *fā'* (فَعْلَتَكَ). No one else read it so.

﴿And you are among the disbelievers﴾, the ones who deny His blessing and the right of [Pharaoh's] upbringing of him: "We raised you among us as a child, and this is how you repay us, by killing one of us and being ungrateful for our blessing." This is the report of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Pharaoh did not know what disbelief in lordship meant.

Moses said: ﴿I did it then, and I was among those astray﴾, i.e., among the ignorant, before any word from God had come to me. This is the view of most exegetes, and it is so also in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and I was among the ignorant."

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ means astray from knowledge that this would lead to his killing.

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ from the right path, without intent, like one who aims at a bird and hits a person.

It is also said: among those in error, like His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your ancient error﴾, and ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾. It is also said: among the forgetful, like His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾.

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ to Midian. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgement﴾, meaning understanding and knowledge, ﴿and made me one of the messengers. And this is a favour with which you reproach me: that you enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾

The scholars differed in its interpretation. Some explained it as an affirmation and others as a denial. Whoever said it is an affirmation said: Moses counted it as a blessing from him to him, in that he raised him and did not kill him as he killed the boys of the Children of Israel, and did not enslave him as he enslaved them, and left me so he did not enslave me. [A note in the second manuscript: "enslaved the Children of Israel," the figurative sense of the verse being: "And this is a favour with which you reproach me: that you enslaved the Children of Israel, and yet you left me and did not enslave me."] This is the view of al-Farra'. Whoever said it is a denial said: its meaning is "and is this a favour?" in the interrogative form, like His saying: ﴿This is my Lord?﴾ (in the sense of a question), and His saying: ﴿So are they the ones who will abide forever?﴾, and the words of the poet:

"...... hum hum" (i.e., "Are they them?")

And 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

"I have not forgotten the day of departure, her standing, and her tears in her eyelids were a flow,
and her saying while the riders were moving: 'You leave us thus and you depart.'"

This is the view of Mujahid. Then they differed as to its meaning. Some said: this is Moses' rejoinder to Pharaoh when he reminded him of the upbringing [he gave him] and said: "If you had not killed the sons of the Children of Israel, my parents would have raised me; so what favour is it of yours upon me?"

It is also said: he mentioned his wrongdoing against the Children of Israel, meaning: "You reproach me that you raised me, yet you forget your crime against the Children of Israel."

It is also said: the meaning is: how do you reproach me with an upbringing when you have enslaved my people? When a people is humiliated, [its members are] humiliated, so your enslaving of the Children of Israel has cancelled your kindness to me.

Al-Hasan said: he says: you took the wealth of the Children of Israel, spent from it on me, and made them slaves.

As for His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾, it means: you took them as slaves. It is said: *'abbadtuhu* and *a'badtuhu* (both meaning "I made him a slave"). Al-Farra' recited:

"Why do my people enslave me, when there are many camels among them that they wish, and slaves?"

This phrase has two possible readings: the first is the accusative, with the preposition removed, meaning: "by your enslaving the Children of Israel." The second is the nominative, in apposition to "favour."

Pharaoh said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, i.e., what is this Lord of the worlds whom you claim you are His messenger to me?

Moses (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you are certain﴾. It is said by al-Kalbi that He created them.

The scholars of meanings (Ahl al-Ma'ani, those who study the meanings of the Qur'an) said: ﴿if you are certain﴾ means: if you see it as you see things with your eyes, then be certain that our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth.

Pharaoh said to those around him, [i.e.,] the nobles of his people. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were five hundred men, wearing bracelets, scheming against the people of Moses, and impressing his own people. ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ Moses, making them understand and enforcing the proof upon them, said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾, speaking words he does not understand and whose soundness he does not know. Moses said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you use reason.﴾

Pharaoh, when the proof was binding upon him and he fell silent without an answer, said out of arrogance towards the truth and persistence in error: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾, the confined.

Al-Kalbi said: his imprisonment was worse than killing, because when he imprisoned a man he would throw him alone in a place, isolated, neither hearing nor seeing anything in it, and he would be cast down into the earth.

When he threatened him with imprisonment, Moses said to him: ﴿Even if I bring you something clear?﴾, something that makes manifest the truth of my words. The meaning of the verse is: "Would you do that if I brought you a clear proof?" Moses said this because it is among human dispositions to incline to fairness and to accept the truth after clarity is made.

Pharaoh said to him: ﴿Then bring it, if you are of the truthful.﴾ Then [Moses] ﴿threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾, its matter plainly manifest. He [Pharaoh] said: "Is there anything other than this?" Then ﴿he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

The scholars of meanings (Ahl al-Ma'ani, those who study the meanings of the Qur'an) said: ﴿if you are certain﴾ means: if you see it as you see things with your eyes, then be certain that our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth.

He [Pharaoh] said: "Is there anything other than this?" Then ﴿he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

i.e., with a message. Al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

meaning "a message," therefore it is said "its destination." This was said by al-Farra'.

It is also said that the meaning is: each of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.

Pharaoh had enslaved them for four hundred years, and at that time they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. Moses set out for Egypt, and Aaron was there, and he informed him of this. Then the doorkeeper entered and said to Pharaoh: "There is a man here who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him." So they both entered upon him and delivered to him the message of God, glory be to Him, and Pharaoh recognised Moses, for he had been raised in his house. It is also said: among those in error, like His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your ancient error﴾, and ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾. It is also said: among the forgetful, like His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾.

The scholars differed in its interpretation. Some explained it as an affirmation and others as a denial. "...... hum hum" (i.e., "Are they them?")

And 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

This is the view of Mujahid. Then they differed as to its meaning. Some said: this is Moses' rejoinder to Pharaoh when he reminded him of the upbringing [he gave him] and said: "If you had not killed the sons of the Children of Israel, my parents would have raised me; so what favour is it of yours upon me?"

It is also said: the meaning is: how do you reproach me with an upbringing when you have enslaved my people? When a people is humiliated, [its members are] humiliated, so your enslaving of the Children of Israel has cancelled your kindness to me.

Pharaoh said to those around him, [i.e.,] the nobles of his people. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were five hundred men, wearing bracelets, scheming against the people of Moses, and impressing his own people. ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ Moses, making them understand and enforcing the proof upon them, said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾, speaking words he does not understand and whose soundness he does not know. Moses said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you use reason.﴾

Pharaoh, when the proof was binding upon him and he fell silent without an answer, said out of arrogance towards the truth and persistence in error: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾, the confined.

Al-Kalbi said: his imprisonment was worse than killing, because when he imprisoned a man he would throw him alone in a place, isolated, neither hearing nor seeing anything in it, and he would be cast down into the earth.

When he threatened him with imprisonment, Moses said to him: ﴿Even if I bring you something clear?﴾, something that makes manifest the truth of my words. The meaning of the verse is: "Would you do that if I brought you a clear proof?" Moses said this because it is among human dispositions to incline to fairness and to accept the truth after clarity is made.

Pharaoh said to him: ﴿Then bring it, if you are of the truthful.﴾ Then [Moses] ﴿threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾, its matter plainly manifest. He [Pharaoh] said: "Is there anything other than this?" Then ﴿he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

And [remember, O Muhammad,] when your Lord called out to Moses when he saw the tree and the fire, saying: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾, those who wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience, and the Children of Israel, whom they enslaved and subjected to a harsh torment.

﴿The people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear God?﴾ Ubayd ibn Umayr read it with the letter *tā'* (تتقون, "will you not fear God?"), meaning: say to them both, "Will you not fear God?"

He said: ﴿My Lord, I fear that they will deny me﴾, and ﴿my breast will be constricted﴾ by their denial of me, ﴿and my tongue will not be loosed﴾ for speech and conveying the message, because of the knot that is in it. The common reading has the two verbs (*yakdhibūn*, *yaḍīqu*) and (*yanṭaliqu*) with *ḍamma* on the *qāf*s, as a continuation of *akhāfu*. Ya'qub read them in the accusative, on the meaning of "that they will deny me, and that my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed." ﴿So send [word] to Aaron﴾ to support me and back me in conveying the message. This is like your saying: "When a calamity befalls me, I send to you," meaning: so that you may help me. ﴿And they have a charge against me﴾, meaning the killing he committed among them. His name was Mathun, and he was Pharaoh's baker. It is also said that the meaning is "with me," i.e., "they have a charge with me." ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ because of it.

God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿No!﴾, meaning: they will not kill you. ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs; indeed We are with you, listening﴾, hearing what they say and what is said to you. He intended by this to strengthen their hearts and to inform them that He would help and protect them. ﴿Go to Pharaoh and say: "Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾

He did not say "messenger" (*rasūlan*, singular) because he meant the verbal noun, i.e., "a message." Its figurative sense is: "one who has a message from the Lord of the worlds," as in the verse of Kuthayyir:

"The slanderers have lied; I did not disclose a secret to them, nor did I send them as a messenger."

i.e., with a message. Al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Except whoever conveys from us to Khafaf, a messenger, the house of your family its destination."

meaning "a message," therefore it is said "its destination." This was said by al-Farra'.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the word *rasūl* may be used for the singular, the dual and the plural. The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent, these two are my messenger and my agent, these are my messenger and my agent." From this is God's saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾. It is also said that the meaning is: each of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.

[Pharaoh is told:] ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., to Palestine, and do not enslave them. Pharaoh had enslaved them for four hundred years, and at that time they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. Moses set out for Egypt, and Aaron was there, and he informed him of this. So they both went together to Pharaoh, but they were not admitted to see him for a year. Then the doorkeeper entered and said to Pharaoh: "There is a man here who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him." So they both entered upon him and delivered to him the message of God, glory be to Him, and Pharaoh recognised Moses, for he had been raised in his house. So he said to him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life﴾, and they were thirty years, ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾, meaning the killing of the Copt.

Ibn 'Abdus informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm related to us, saying: al-Farra' related to us, saying: Musa al-Ansari related to me, from al-Sari ibn Isma'il, from al-Sha'bi, that he read ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾ with a *kasra* on the *fā'* (فَعْلَتَكَ). No one else read it so.

﴿And you are among the disbelievers﴾, the ones who deny His blessing and the right of [Pharaoh's] upbringing of him: "We raised you among us as a child, and this is how you repay us, by killing one of us and being ungrateful for our blessing." This is the report of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Pharaoh did not know what disbelief in lordship meant.

Moses said: ﴿I did it then, and I was among those astray﴾, i.e., among the ignorant, before any word from God had come to me. This is the view of most exegetes, and it is so also in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and I was among the ignorant."

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ means astray from knowledge that this would lead to his killing.

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ from the right path, without intent, like one who aims at a bird and hits a person.

It is also said: among those in error, like His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your ancient error﴾, and ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾. It is also said: among the forgetful, like His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾.

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ to Midian. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgement﴾, meaning understanding and knowledge, ﴿and made me one of the messengers. And this is a favour with which you reproach me: that you enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾

The scholars differed in its interpretation. Some explained it as an affirmation and others as a denial. Whoever said it is an affirmation said: Moses counted it as a blessing from him to him, in that he raised him and did not kill him as he killed the boys of the Children of Israel, and did not enslave him as he enslaved them, and left me so he did not enslave me. [A note in the second manuscript: "enslaved the Children of Israel," the figurative sense of the verse being: "And this is a favour with which you reproach me: that you enslaved the Children of Israel, and yet you left me and did not enslave me."] This is the view of al-Farra'. Whoever said it is a denial said: its meaning is "and is this a favour?" in the interrogative form, like His saying: ﴿This is my Lord?﴾ (in the sense of a question), and His saying: ﴿So are they the ones who will abide forever?﴾, and the words of the poet:

"...... hum hum" (i.e., "Are they them?")

And 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

"I have not forgotten the day of departure, her standing, and her tears in her eyelids were a flow,
and her saying while the riders were moving: 'You leave us thus and you depart.'"

This is the view of Mujahid. Then they differed as to its meaning. Some said: this is Moses' rejoinder to Pharaoh when he reminded him of the upbringing [he gave him] and said: "If you had not killed the sons of the Children of Israel, my parents would have raised me; so what favour is it of yours upon me?"

It is also said: he mentioned his wrongdoing against the Children of Israel, meaning: "You reproach me that you raised me, yet you forget your crime against the Children of Israel."

It is also said: the meaning is: how do you reproach me with an upbringing when you have enslaved my people? When a people is humiliated, [its members are] humiliated, so your enslaving of the Children of Israel has cancelled your kindness to me.

Al-Hasan said: he says: you took the wealth of the Children of Israel, spent from it on me, and made them slaves.

Then the doorkeeper entered and said to Pharaoh: "There is a man here who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him." So they both entered upon him and delivered to him the message of God, glory be to Him, and Pharaoh recognised Moses, for he had been raised in his house. So he said to him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life﴾, and they were thirty years, ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾, meaning the killing of the Copt.

No one else read it so.

﴿And you are among the disbelievers﴾, the ones who deny His blessing and the right of [Pharaoh's] upbringing of him: "We raised you among us as a child, and this is how you repay us, by killing one of us and being ungrateful for our blessing." This is the report of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Pharaoh did not know what disbelief in lordship meant.

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ from the right path, without intent, like one who aims at a bird and hits a person.

It is also said: among those in error, like His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your ancient error﴾, and ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾. It is also said: among the forgetful, like His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾.

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ to Midian. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgement﴾, meaning understanding and knowledge, ﴿and made me one of the messengers. And this is a favour with which you reproach me: that you enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾

The scholars differed in its interpretation. Some explained it as an affirmation and others as a denial. Whoever said it is an affirmation said: Moses counted it as a blessing from him to him, in that he raised him and did not kill him as he killed the boys of the Children of Israel, and did not enslave him as he enslaved them, and left me so he did not enslave me. Whoever said it is a denial said: its meaning is "and is this a favour?" in the interrogative form, like His saying: ﴿This is my Lord?﴾ (in the sense of a question), and His saying: ﴿So are they the ones who will abide forever?﴾, and the words of the poet:

"...... hum hum" (i.e., "Are they them?")

And 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

"I have not forgotten the day of departure, her standing, and her tears in her eyelids were a flow,
and her saying while the riders were moving: 'You leave us thus and you depart.'"

This is the view of Mujahid. Then they differed as to its meaning. Some said: this is Moses' rejoinder to Pharaoh when he reminded him of the upbringing [he gave him] and said: "If you had not killed the sons of the Children of Israel, my parents would have raised me; so what favour is it of yours upon me?"

It is also said: he mentioned his wrongdoing against the Children of Israel, meaning: "You reproach me that you raised me, yet you forget your crime against the Children of Israel."

It is also said: the meaning is: how do you reproach me with an upbringing when you have enslaved my people? When a people is humiliated, [its members are] humiliated, so your enslaving of the Children of Israel has cancelled your kindness to me.

Al-Hasan said: he says: you took the wealth of the Children of Israel, spent from it on me, and made them slaves.

As for His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾, it means: you took them as slaves. It is said: *'abbadtuhu* and *a'badtuhu* (both meaning "I made him a slave"). Al-Farra' recited:

"Why do my people enslave me, when there are many camels among them that they wish, and slaves?"

This phrase has two possible readings: the first is the accusative, with the preposition removed, meaning: "by your enslaving the Children of Israel." The second is the nominative, in apposition to "favour."

Pharaoh said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, i.e., what is this Lord of the worlds whom you claim you are His messenger to me?

Moses (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you are certain﴾. It is said by al-Kalbi that He created them.

The scholars of meanings (Ahl al-Ma'ani, those who study the meanings of the Qur'an) said: ﴿if you are certain﴾ means: if you see it as you see things with your eyes, then be certain that our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth.

Pharaoh said to those around him, [i.e.,] the nobles of his people. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were five hundred men, wearing bracelets, scheming against the people of Moses, and impressing his own people. ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ Moses, making them understand and enforcing the proof upon them, said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾, speaking words he does not understand and whose soundness he does not know. Moses said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you use reason.﴾

Pharaoh, when the proof was binding upon him and he fell silent without an answer, said out of arrogance towards the truth and persistence in error: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾, the confined.

Al-Kalbi said: his imprisonment was worse than killing, because when he imprisoned a man he would throw him alone in a place, isolated, neither hearing nor seeing anything in it, and he would be cast down into the earth.

Moses said this because it is among human dispositions to incline to fairness and to accept the truth after clarity is made.

He [Pharaoh] said: "Is there anything other than this?" Then ﴿he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

i.e., with a message. Al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

His name was Mathun, and he was Pharaoh's baker. It is also said that the meaning is "with me," i.e., "they have a charge with me." ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ because of it.

God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿No!﴾, meaning: they will not kill you. ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs; indeed We are with you, listening﴾, hearing what they say and what is said to you. He intended by this to strengthen their hearts and to inform them that He would help and protect them. ﴿Go to Pharaoh and say: "Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾

He did not say "messenger" (*rasūlan*, singular) because he meant the verbal noun, i.e., "a message." Its figurative sense is: "one who has a message from the Lord of the worlds," as in the verse of Kuthayyir:

i.e., with a message. Al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

meaning "a message," therefore it is said "its destination." This was said by al-Farra'.

The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent, these two are my messenger and my agent, these are my messenger and my agent." From this is God's saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾. It is also said that the meaning is: each of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.

[Pharaoh is told:] ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., to Palestine, and do not enslave them. Pharaoh had enslaved them for four hundred years, and at that time they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. Moses set out for Egypt, and Aaron was there, and he informed him of this. So they both went together to Pharaoh, but they were not admitted to see him for a year. Then the doorkeeper entered and said to Pharaoh: "There is a man here who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him." So they both entered upon him and delivered to him the message of God, glory be to Him, and Pharaoh recognised Moses, for he had been raised in his house. So he said to him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life﴾, and they were thirty years, ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾, meaning the killing of the Copt.

Ibn 'Abdus informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm related to us, saying: al-Farra' related to us, saying: Musa al-Ansari related to me, from al-Sari ibn Isma'il, from al-Sha'bi, that he read ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾ with a *kasra* on the *fā'* (فَعْلَتَكَ). No one else read it so.

﴿And you are among the disbelievers﴾, the ones who deny His blessing and the right of [Pharaoh's] upbringing of him: "We raised you among us as a child, and this is how you repay us, by killing one of us and being ungrateful for our blessing." This is the report of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Pharaoh did not know what disbelief in lordship meant.

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ means astray from knowledge that this would lead to his killing.

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ from the right path, without intent, like one who aims at a bird and hits a person.

It is also said: among those in error, like His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your ancient error﴾, and ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾. It is also said: among the forgetful, like His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾.

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ to Midian. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgement﴾, meaning understanding and knowledge, ﴿and made me one of the messengers. And this is a favour with which you reproach me: that you enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾

The scholars differed in its interpretation. Some explained it as an affirmation and others as a denial. Whoever said it is an affirmation said: Moses counted it as a blessing from him to him, in that he raised him and did not kill him as he killed the boys of the Children of Israel, and did not enslave him as he enslaved them, and left me so he did not enslave me. Whoever said it is a denial said: its meaning is "and is this a favour?" in the interrogative form, like His saying: ﴿This is my Lord?﴾ (in the sense of a question), and His saying: ﴿So are they the ones who will abide forever?﴾, and the words of the poet:

"...... hum hum" (i.e., "Are they them?")

And 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

"I have not forgotten the day of departure, her standing, and her tears in her eyelids were a flow,
and her saying while the riders were moving: 'You leave us thus and you depart.'"

This is the view of Mujahid. Then they differed as to its meaning. Some said: this is Moses' rejoinder to Pharaoh when he reminded him of the upbringing [he gave him] and said: "If you had not killed the sons of the Children of Israel, my parents would have raised me; so what favour is it of yours upon me?"

It is also said: he mentioned his wrongdoing against the Children of Israel, meaning: "You reproach me that you raised me, yet you forget your crime against the Children of Israel."

It is also said: the meaning is: how do you reproach me with an upbringing when you have enslaved my people? When a people is humiliated, [its members are] humiliated, so your enslaving of the Children of Israel has cancelled your kindness to me.

Al-Hasan said: he says: you took the wealth of the Children of Israel, spent from it on me, and made them slaves.

The scholars of meanings (Ahl al-Ma'ani, those who study the meanings of the Qur'an) said: ﴿if you are certain﴾ means: if you see it as you see things with your eyes, then be certain that our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth.

He [Pharaoh] said: "Is there anything other than this?" Then ﴿he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

Pharaoh said to those around him, [i.e.,] the nobles of his people. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were five hundred men, wearing bracelets, scheming against the people of Moses, and impressing his own people. ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ Moses, making them understand and enforcing the proof upon them, said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾, speaking words he does not understand and whose soundness he does not know. Moses said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you use reason.﴾

Pharaoh, when the proof was binding upon him and he fell silent without an answer, said out of arrogance towards the truth and persistence in error: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾, the confined.

Al-Kalbi said: his imprisonment was worse than killing, because when he imprisoned a man he would throw him alone in a place, isolated, neither hearing nor seeing anything in it, and he would be cast down into the earth.

When he threatened him with imprisonment, Moses said to him: ﴿Even if I bring you something clear?﴾, something that makes manifest the truth of my words. The meaning of the verse is: "Would you do that if I brought you a clear proof?" Moses said this because it is among human dispositions to incline to fairness and to accept the truth after clarity is made.

Pharaoh said to him: ﴿Then bring it, if you are of the truthful.﴾ Then [Moses] ﴿threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾, its matter plainly manifest. He [Pharaoh] said: "Is there anything other than this?" Then ﴿he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

And [remember, O Muhammad,] when your Lord called out to Moses when he saw the tree and the fire, saying: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾, those who wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience, and the Children of Israel, whom they enslaved and subjected to a harsh torment.

﴿The people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear God?﴾ Ubayd ibn Umayr read it with the letter *tā'* (تتقون, "will you not fear God?"), meaning: say to them both, "Will you not fear God?"

He said: ﴿My Lord, I fear that they will deny me﴾, and ﴿my breast will be constricted﴾ by their denial of me, ﴿and my tongue will not be loosed﴾ for speech and conveying the message, because of the knot that is in it. The common reading has the two verbs (*yakdhibūn*, *yaḍīqu*) and (*yanṭaliqu*) with *ḍamma* on the *qāf*s, as a continuation of *akhāfu*. Ya'qub read them in the accusative, on the meaning of "that they will deny me, and that my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed." ﴿So send [word] to Aaron﴾ to support me and back me in conveying the message. This is like your saying: "When a calamity befalls me, I send to you," meaning: so that you may help me. ﴿And they have a charge against me﴾, meaning the killing he committed among them. His name was Mathun, and he was Pharaoh's baker. It is also said that the meaning is "with me," i.e., "they have a charge with me." ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ because of it.

God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿No!﴾, meaning: they will not kill you. ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs; indeed We are with you, listening﴾, hearing what they say and what is said to you. He intended by this to strengthen their hearts and to inform them that He would help and protect them. ﴿Go to Pharaoh and say: "Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾

He did not say "messenger" (*rasūlan*, singular) because he meant the verbal noun, i.e., "a message." Its figurative sense is: "one who has a message from the Lord of the worlds," as in the verse of Kuthayyir:

"The slanderers have lied; I did not disclose a secret to them, nor did I send them as a messenger."

i.e., with a message. Al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Except whoever conveys from us to Khafaf, a messenger, the house of your family its destination."

meaning "a message," therefore it is said "its destination." This was said by al-Farra'.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the word *rasūl* may be used for the singular, the dual and the plural. The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent, these two are my messenger and my agent, these are my messenger and my agent." From this is God's saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾. It is also said that the meaning is: each of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.

[Pharaoh is told:] ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., to Palestine, and do not enslave them. Pharaoh had enslaved them for four hundred years, and at that time they numbered six hundred and thirty thousand. Moses set out for Egypt, and Aaron was there, and he informed him of this. So they both went together to Pharaoh, but they were not admitted to see him for a year. Then the doorkeeper entered and said to Pharaoh: "There is a man here who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him." So they both entered upon him and delivered to him the message of God, glory be to Him, and Pharaoh recognised Moses, for he had been raised in his house. So he said to him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life﴾, and they were thirty years, ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾, meaning the killing of the Copt.

Ibn 'Abdus informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm related to us, saying: al-Farra' related to us, saying: Musa al-Ansari related to me, from al-Sari ibn Isma'il, from al-Sha'bi, that he read ﴿and you did your deed which you did﴾ with a *kasra* on the *fā'* (فَعْلَتَكَ). No one else read it so.

﴿And you are among the disbelievers﴾, the ones who deny His blessing and the right of [Pharaoh's] upbringing of him: "We raised you among us as a child, and this is how you repay us, by killing one of us and being ungrateful for our blessing." This is the report of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Pharaoh did not know what disbelief in lordship meant.

Moses said: ﴿I did it then, and I was among those astray﴾, i.e., among the ignorant, before any word from God had come to me. This is the view of most exegetes, and it is so also in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and I was among the ignorant."

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ means astray from knowledge that this would lead to his killing.

It is also said: ﴿among those astray﴾ from the right path, without intent, like one who aims at a bird and hits a person.

It is also said: among those in error, like His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your ancient error﴾, and ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾. It is also said: among the forgetful, like His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾.

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ to Midian. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgement﴾, meaning understanding and knowledge, ﴿and made me one of the messengers. And this is a favour with which you reproach me: that you enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾

The scholars differed in its interpretation. Some explained it as an affirmation and others as a denial. Whoever said it is an affirmation said: Moses counted it as a blessing from him to him, in that he raised him and did not kill him as he killed the boys of the Children of Israel, and did not enslave him as he enslaved them, and left me so he did not enslave me. [A note in the second manuscript: "enslaved the Children of Israel," the figurative sense of the verse being: "And this is a favour with which you reproach me: that you enslaved the Children of Israel, and yet you left me and did not enslave me."] This is the view of al-Farra'. Whoever said it is a denial said: its meaning is "and is this a favour?" in the interrogative form, like His saying: ﴿This is my Lord?﴾ (in the sense of a question), and His saying: ﴿So are they the ones who will abide forever?﴾, and the words of the poet:

"...... hum hum" (i.e., "Are they them?")

And 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

"I have not forgotten the day of departure, her standing, and her tears in her eyelids were a flow,
and her saying while the riders were moving: 'You leave us thus and you depart.'"

This is the view of Mujahid. Then they differed as to its meaning. Some said: this is Moses' rejoinder to Pharaoh when he reminded him of the upbringing [he gave him] and said: "If you had not killed the sons of the Children of Israel, my parents would have raised me; so what favour is it of yours upon me?"

It is also said: he mentioned his wrongdoing against the Children of Israel, meaning: "You reproach me that you raised me, yet you forget your crime against the Children of Israel."

It is also said: the meaning is: how do you reproach me with an upbringing when you have enslaved my people? When a people is humiliated, [its members are] humiliated, so your enslaving of the Children of Israel has cancelled your kindness to me.

Al-Hasan said: he says: you took the wealth of the Children of Israel, spent from it on me, and made them slaves.

Some said: this is Moses' rejoinder to Pharaoh when he reminded him of the upbringing [he gave him] and said: "If you had not killed the sons of the Children of Israel, my parents would have raised me; so what favour is it of yours upon me?"

It is also said: he mentioned his wrongdoing against the Children of Israel, meaning: "You reproach me that you raised me, yet you forget your crime against the Children of Israel."

It is also said: the meaning is: how do you reproach me with an upbringing when you have enslaved my people? When a people is humiliated, [its members are] humiliated, so your enslaving of the Children of Israel has cancelled your kindness to me.

This phrase has two possible readings: the first is the accusative, with the preposition removed, meaning: "by your enslaving the Children of Israel." The second is the nominative, in apposition to "favour."

Ibn 'Abbas said: they were five hundred men, wearing bracelets, scheming against the people of Moses, and impressing his own people. ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ Moses, making them understand and enforcing the proof upon them, said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾, speaking words he does not understand and whose soundness he does not know. He [Pharaoh] said: "Is there anything other than this?" Then ﴿he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

i.e., with a message. Al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

meaning "a message," therefore it is said "its destination." This was said by al-Farra'.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 26, verses 34–68:

Pharaoh said to the chiefs around him: ﴿Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer. He intends to drive you out of your land with his sorcery. So what do you advise?﴾ They said: ﴿Put him off, and his brother, and send heralds into the cities to bring you every skilled sorcerer.﴾ So the sorcerers were gathered for an appointed time on a known day, and it was the Day of Adornment (yawm al-zina).

Ibn 'Abbas said: That day coincided with a Saturday, the first day of the year, and it was the day of Nawruz (the Persian New Year).

Ibn Zayd said: Their gathering for the appointed time was in Alexandria. It is also said: the tail of the serpent reached beyond the lake that day.

And it was said to the people: ﴿Will you gather, so that you may watch what the two parties do, and so that we may follow the sorcerers if they are the victors?﴾ It was said that they meant this in mockery, and by "the sorcerers" they meant Musa, Harun and their people.

When the sorcerers came, they said to Pharaoh: ﴿Will we surely have a reward if we are the victors?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, and you will then be among those brought near.﴾ Musa said to them: ﴿Throw what you are going to throw.﴾ So they threw their ropes and their staffs, and said: ﴿By the might of Pharaoh, we are surely the victors.﴾ Then Musa threw his staff, and behold, it swallowed what they had falsely produced. So the sorcerers fell down prostrating, and said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun.﴾ He said: ﴿Do you believe in Him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. You will soon know. I will surely cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all.﴾ They said: ﴿No harm. Indeed, we are returning to our Lord. We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we are the first of the believers.﴾ And We revealed to Musa: ﴿Travel by night with My servants; indeed, you will be pursued.﴾ (That is, Pharaoh and his people will pursue you.)

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Lu'lu' narrated to us, saying: al-Haytham ibn Khalaf informed us, saying: al-Dawraqi narrated to us, from Hajjaj ibn Jurayj, regarding this verse, that he said: Allah, glorified is He, revealed to Musa: "Gather the Children of Israel, every four households in one house. Then slaughter lambs and strike their blood upon your property, for I will command the angels so that they will not enter a house upon whose door there is blood. I will command them to kill the firstborn of the family of Pharaoh, from among their own persons and their wealth. Then bake unleavened bread, for it is quicker for you. Then travel by night with My servants until you reach the sea, and My command will come to you." He did so. When they woke in the morning, Pharaoh said: "This is the deed of Musa and his people. They have killed our firstborn from among ourselves and our wealth." So he sent into his affair one million and five hundred thousand crowned kings, with each king having a thousand. Pharaoh went out in the great throne.
